thread.title: General Electric Capitulates To $8.15 On JPMorgan Downgrade. Time To Buy? - General Electric (NYSE:GE)

author: Giovanni DiMauro
title: General Electric Capitulates To $8.15 On JPMorgan Downgrade. Time To Buy? - General Electric (NYSE:GE)
text:
Beleaguered General Electric ( GE ) shareholders faced another gut check Friday when JPMorgan's Stephen Tusa cut the price target to $6 . Tusa is predicting that by 2020 the company will have six segments producing zero free cash flow.
Here is what Tusa had to say about the GE debacle.
"Out of the 8 reported segments, all of which were profitable even 2 years ago, 6 are now likely either at or below zero in 2020, with leverage actually up since that time.
"In other words, we estimate material dilution from weak fundamentals and portfolio moves, with little in return, going against the notion from a year ago that the company could get $20 [billion] in value without diluting the run rate of earnings/FCF."
"While the stock is down 70% from the peak of $30, this move still does not sufficiently reflect the fundamental facts, in our view."
"While liquidity is certainly debatable, we believe this is not really about liquidity, it's about a deterioration in run rate fundamentals."
It's no secret that Tusa has been spot on with GE and with good reason. GE has failed to come close to guidance of $1.05 to 1.10 that was forecasted earlier this year. Will GE trade down to $6? Maybe, that will depend on whether there are any more big shoes to drop.
What will GE earn in 2019?
Investors did not get any firm guidance on the last conference call. Tusa is expecting earnings of $0.35 cents a share for 2019 and $0.41 for 2020. The street was looking for nearly twice that number.
I have no idea if GE will earn $0.40 for 2020 because I don't believe management has a handle on how severe or long the downturn will last in the Power segment. My main concern is the loss of revenue from the power division along with pension liabilities and the possibility of GE Capital's need for more liquidity.
Why I sold my recently purchased shares on Thursday after studying the 10Q.
I wrote an article last weekend titled "GE in Capitulation Time to Buy?" You can read that piece here .
I spent a few hours reading the 10Q: I am not an accountant, I don't play one on TV and I did not spent the night in a Holiday Inn Express last night. That being said, I did not like what I read about GE Capital.
Reading a 10Q from General Electric is enough to give you a headache and serious indigestion if your holding a large position. On Wednesday I bought several thousand shares between $9.16 - $9.22 thinking I just might have nailed the bottom.
Later that afternoon I decided to dig deeper into the 10Q for a 2nd time. Power division losses and GE Capital's lack of clarity sealed the deal for me. I decided to get out as I was sure Tusa would come out and hit GE hard with another downgrade. I sold 30% of my position at the close on Wednesday and went to bed worried about the next possible gap down.
Needless to say I dumped my whole position Thursday morning from $9.18 to $9.26 per share. I was out of the trade by 6:40 AM for a loss around a $100, I felt lucky.
Little did I know that the next day the dreaded $6 call would come from JPMorgan's Tusa. GE gapped down to open at $8.79, within 2 hours it bottomed at $8.15 and slowly gained ground to close the day at a decade low of $8.58.
Seeing GE trade at $8.21 today and not buying was actually very difficult for this trader. It felt like capitulation; however, in this case I did not pull the trigger as I have no trust in management's ability to fix GE any time soon.
Is GE Capital going to need another cash infusion from GE?
In 2017 GE received a $4B dividend from GE Capital. In 2018 the dividend was suspended. In the latest earnings announcement management revealed that GE Capital's insurance legacy division would need $14B to add to reserves.
This is from page 29 of the 10Q .
In my view, this is an issue that must be clarified by management. I highly encourage anyone considering investing in this stock to read this page and then crack open the 10Q and have a look.
How much more liquidity could be required over the next few years?
GE now finds itself in a situation where they went from receiving a dividend the first 9 months of 2017 of $4B to ZERO. GE Capital expects to make no dividend contributions for the foreseeable future. This is not good for GE or shareholders, GE needed that cash flow to fund operations and now its gone.
To make matters worse, GE had to contribute $3.5B of capital to the insurance division and will need to contribute another $11B through 2024. Continue on and you will read that the Kansas Insurance Dept. could increase or decrease reserves depending on premium deficiency.
It's entirely possible that the company would have to pay well beyond the $11B noted above. That is a huge swing; GE loses $4B a year in dividends for 6 years which equals $24B. GE Capital will require a contribution of $14.5B through 2024 at a minimum. That is $38.5B in lost cash flow over a 6 year time frame.
These are old insurance policies that the company is stuck with. People are living longer than ever before and the insurance costs go up all the time. I believe it is important to note that for every 5% increase in costs of future claims could result in another $1.5B increase to future policy benefit reserves.
Where does it stop? Will management actually come clean and inform shareholders of the absolute worst case scenario so investors and analysts can get a grip on the magnitude of the problem?
This is a can of worms that I want no part of as an investor. I really wanted to believe in GE as an iconic American Company; that dream for me is dead.
In my view their accounting practices leave a lot to be desired.
I see lawsuits as far as the eye can see.
GE is facing multiple class action lawsuits from investors that feel they were mislead by previous management's guidance.
Every quarterly earnings release seems to make the case stronger for the plaintiffs. GE has caused massive pain for many a weary shareholder. At some point they are going to have to pay. How much? Only the shadow knows at this point.
The SEC is investigating GE's accounting practice and insurance division. The justice Dept. is investigating the subprime mortgage division . Both of these investigations creates uncertainty which is likely to keep a dark cloud over the stock for the next 12 to 18 months.
CEO Larry Culp buys $2.2M worth of shares.
Larry Culp bought 225,000 shares for an average price of $9.73 this week . While some investors may take this as a bullish sign, it is important to note that many companies require an incoming CEO to take a substantial position.
Mr. Culp is now upside down $1.15 a share, or $258,750 to be exact. If he really wants to make a statement to the market, he could buy $10 million of shares on Monday morning at or near the current level. I believe that would get the attention of the street and inspire confidence among some investors.
Is GE going to turn it around any time soon?
Not in the next 12 months, but that doesn't mean the stock cannot bounce hard.
Did GE bottom today? Maybe, the bottoming process takes time. Today was likely the first salvo in several attempts to break $8. The stock could take off and rally back to $11. A more likely scenario is the dreaded year end tax loss selling which could continue to pressure the stock.
Here's a look at a 10 year weekly chart.
Everyone wants to buy the absolute bottom on a big name like GE. It's not hard to see why Tusa hit GE with a $6 target, look at the chart. He is gunning for a total round trip retest of the March 2009 low. It looks like capitulation right here and now. The fact that I do not want to own it might be proof, but I digress.
Management must do a better job of communicating
Larry Culp has a very limited amount of time to stop the bleeding and be very straight forward with shareholders. GE Capital needs to be discussed in an open forum with clear and precise communication.
Bottom Line
GE is in the dog house, investors are fleeing the name because they do not trust management. Fool me once, shame on you, fool me twice, shame on me.
I am not even going to consider this company until Larry Culp can take control and communicate exactly what is happening with GE Capital's legacy insurance liabilities.
GE has no clarity in GE Capital, no profits and no dividend to pay investors while they wait. Every earnings report brings a multi billion dollar write down or impairment charge.
Why not look at a company that is making all time record profits like Apple ( AAPL )? Apple is a complete opposite of GE, delivering record high profits in all segments, on every metric.
Trust is my main issue here, I have none for GE.
As always, do your own research, crack open a 10Q and study. I believe it is imperative to have an exit strategy in place before making any trade;it can help keep you grounded in times of high volatility.
Disclosure: I/we have no positions in any stocks mentioned, and no plans to initiate any positions within the next 72 hours.
